questions.q: What is the default alignment for text and numeric values in an Excel cell before any formatting is applied?
questions.a: By default, text is left-aligned and numeric values (including dates and times) are right-aligned in a cell. A wrong answer (e.g., "both are centered" or "text is right-aligned") reveals that the student has not observed the default behavior, which is critical because many formatting decisions (like applying Center alignment to headers only) depend on knowing the starting state.

questions.q: A student enters `12/04/2024` in a cell and sees `12-Apr-2024` displayed. They then apply the "Number" format with 2 decimal places and see `45386.00`. Explain why the displayed value changed and what the number `45386` represents.
questions.a: Excel stores dates as serial numbers where 1 = 1-Jan-1900; `45386` is the number of days since that epoch for 12-Apr-2024. Changing the format to Number reveals the underlying stored value. A student who says "the date got corrupted" or "Excel converted it wrongly" misunderstands that formatting only changes *display*, not the stored value — a core concept for later work with date arithmetic and conditional formatting on dates.

questions.q: You have a column of profit margins (e.g., 0.12, 0.05, -0.03, 0.18). You want to display them as percentages with one decimal (12.0%, 5.0%, -3.0%, 18.0%) and highlight any negative margin in red font with a red fill. Describe the exact sequence of steps using the Ribbon (no shortcuts) to achieve both.
questions.a: 1. Select the range. 2. Home → Number group → click % (Percent Style) → click Increase Decimal once. 3. Home → Conditional Formatting → Highlight Cells Rules → Less Than → enter `0` → choose "Light Red Fill with Dark Red Text" → OK. A student who applies the red fill *before* percentage formatting may not realize the condition `Less Than 0` works on the underlying decimal (0.12, -0.03), not the displayed percentage — both work, but understanding the stored value is key for complex rules.

questions.q: Compare "Format as Table" (Home → Styles → Format as Table) with manually applying banded row fill colors via Conditional Formatting → New Rule → Use a formula `=MOD(ROW(),2)=0`. Which method is more robust when rows are inserted or deleted, and why?
questions.a: "Format as Table" is more robust because it creates a structured Table object (ListObject) that automatically maintains banded rows, filter buttons, and structured references when rows are added/removed. The Conditional Formatting formula approach breaks if rows are inserted above the range (ROW() shifts) or if the range is not updated. A student who prefers the formula method may not grasp that Tables are dynamic objects, not just formatting — a critical distinction for data integrity in accounting.

questions.q: A colleague sends you a workbook where the "Total Sales" column shows `#####` in several cells. You widen the column and the numbers appear. The colleague insists the data was "fixed" by widening. Evaluate this claim: is the data actually fixed? What would you check to be sure?
questions.a: The claim is false: `#####` is a *display* error (column too narrow or negative date/time), not a data error. The underlying values are intact. To verify, check the Formula Bar for a `#####` cell — it will show the actual number. Also check if any cell contains a negative date/time (e.g., `=A1-B1` where A1<B1) which also shows `#####` regardless of width. A student who thinks widening "fixes" the data confuses presentation with data integrity — dangerous in accounting where hidden negatives matter.

questions.q: Design a conditional formatting rule (using a formula) for a range `B5:B100` (invoice amounts) that highlights the entire row (A5:F5, A6:F6, ...) in yellow if the invoice amount is greater than the average of all invoices in B5:B100 AND the invoice date in column A is in the current month. Write the formula for the rule applied to `A5:F100`.
questions.a: `=AND($B5>AVERAGE($B$5:$B$100), MONTH($A5)=MONTH(TODAY()), YEAR($A5)=YEAR(TODAY()))` applied to `A5:F100`. The formula uses mixed references: column locked ($B, $A) so the condition travels across columns, row relative (5) so it evaluates per row. A student who writes `=$B5>AVERAGE(B5:B100)` without absolute references for the average range will get a shifting average — a classic error showing misunderstanding of reference locking in conditional formatting formulas.
